The author’s preface: In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful
The servant who is in need of God the Exalted and rich through His kindness, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad ibn Khaldūn al-Ḥaḍramī, may God grant him success, says:

Praise be to God, to whom belong might and omnipotence; in whose hand are kingship and dominion; to whom belong the most beautiful names and the attributes; the Knowing, from whom nothing escapes, whether whispered counsel reveals it or silence conceals it; the Powerful, whom nothing in the heavens and the earth can defeat and from whom nothing slips away. He brought us forth from the earth as living souls, had us settle on it as generations and nations, and made provisions and portions from it easy for us. Wombs and houses enfold us; sustenance and food provide for us; days and appointed times wear us out; and the terms of our lives, whose appointed record has been written down against us, befall us in turn. To Him belong permanence and constancy, and He is the Living who does not die. Blessings and peace be upon our lord and master Muḥammad, the Arab Prophet, who is written of in the Torah and the Gospel and described there, for whose birth the universe labored before Sundays and Saturdays followed one another and before Saturn and the Behemoth (al-Yahmūt) became distinct; and upon his family and Companions, who, in keeping his company and following him, have a far-reaching influence and renown, and a united fellowship in supporting him, while their enemy’s fellowship is scattered. God bless him and them for as long as the lucky fortune of Islam remains attached to it and the cord of unbelief remains cut off, and grant them abundant peace.

Now then: the art of history is one of those arts that nations and generations pass among themselves, for which travelers saddle their mounts and set out on journeys, to knowing which commoners and the obscure aspire, in which kings and princes compete, and in understanding which scholars and the ignorant are equal. For in its outward aspect it amounts to nothing more than reports about days and dynasties and about earlier things from the first centuries — reports in which sayings multiply and proverbs are coined, with which gatherings are delighted when they are crowded, and which convey to us the condition of creation: how circumstances turned about for it, how wide a range and field dynasties had in it, how they peopled the earth until departure called out to them and the time of their passing came. In its inner aspect it is reflection and verification, a subtle explanation of created things and their origins, and a profound knowledge of how events happened and why. For this reason it is deeply rooted in philosophy, and it deserves and merits to be counted among its sciences.

The foremost historians of Islam have indeed covered the reports of the days fully and collected them, set them down in the pages of their volumes and deposited them there. But interlopers mixed them with insidious falsehoods in which they erred and which they invented, and with embellishments drawn from weak narrations that they pieced together and forged. Many of those who came after them followed those traces and went along with them, and handed the reports on to us just as they had heard them. They did not notice the causes of events and conditions or take them into account, and they neither rejected idle tales nor repelled them. So verification is scarce, the eye of critical revision is for the most part dull, error and delusion are kin and companion to reports, uncritical imitation is deeply rooted in human beings and descended from them, meddling in the arts is wide and long-lasting, and the pasture of ignorance among mankind is unhealthy and deadly. Yet the sovereignty of truth cannot be resisted, and falsehood’s devil is pelted with the shooting star of reflection. The transmitter merely dictates and transmits, but insight sifts out what is sound when it looks closely, and knowledge clears and burnishes for it the pages of hearts.

Moreover, people have recorded a great deal in the way of reports and have been prolific; they have collected the histories of the nations and dynasties of the world and set them down in writing. But those who carried off the distinction of fame and recognized leadership, and who drained the registers of those before them into their own later volumes, are few, hardly exceeding the number of fingers or of the vowel movements produced by the grammatical governors. They include Ibn Isḥāq, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn al-Kalbī, Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar al-Wāqidī, Sayf ibn ʿUmar al-Asadī, and others of the well known, who stand out from the masses. Even though there is, in the books of al-Masʿūdī and al-Wāqidī, a degree of impeachment and aspersion that is known to the reliable authorities and well known among the trustworthy memorizers, everyone has singled these authors out for acceptance of their reports, for following their ways of composition and going after their traces. The discerning critic is his own scale in discrediting what they transmit or in crediting them. For civilization has natures in its conditions to which reports are referred, and by which narrations and traditions are judged.

Then, most of these authors’ histories follow general methods and approaches, because the two dynasties of early Islam were universal in extent across the regions and realms, and reached distant limits in what they took and what they left alone. Among these authors are some who covered the dynasties and nations that preceded the faith, the entire matter without exception, like al-Masʿūdī and those who followed his course. After them came those who turned from the unrestricted to the restricted and stopped short of the far goal in universality and comprehensiveness: they recorded the stray matters of their age, covered the reports of their own horizon and region, and confined themselves to the history of their own dynasty and city, as Abū Ḥayyān, the historian of al-Andalus and of the Umayyad dynasty there, did, and Ibn al-Rafīq, the historian of Ifrīqiya and of the dynasty that was in Qayrawān.

Then after these came only imitators, dull of nature and mind — thoroughly dull — who weave on that same loom and follow its model, and who are oblivious to the conditions that the days have transformed and to the customs of nations and generations that they have put in their place. So they import reports about dynasties and tales of events in the first ages: forms stripped of their materials, swords drawn from their sheaths, and items of knowledge that are found strange because their recent and their ancestral parts are unknown. They are merely occurrences whose origins are not known, and species whose genera have not been taken into account and whose differentiae have not been established. In their compositions they repeat the circulating reports exactly as they are, following those of their predecessors who concerned themselves with them, and they neglect the matter of the emerging generations in its record, because they lack an interpreter of it, so that their pages are mute about explaining it. Then, when they take up the mention of a dynasty, they string its reports together in a series, keeping to the transmission, whether in error or in truth. They do not address its beginning, nor mention the cause that raised its banner and made its sign manifest, nor the reason for its stopping at its limit. So the reader is still left eager to find out the conditions of the beginnings of dynasties and their ranks, searching for the causes of their crowding one another or succeeding one another, and looking for something satisfying about their divergence or their correspondence, as we shall mention all of that in the Introduction to the book. Then others came with excessive brevity, going so far as to be content with the names of kings and to limit themselves to them, cut off from genealogies and reports, with the number of their days set down beside them in dust letters, as Ibn Rashīq did in Mīzān al-ʿamal (“The Balance of Action”), and those of the rabble who followed this trail. No statement of theirs is taken into account, and neither fixity nor movement is counted for them, because of the benefits they have thrown away and because they have neglected the well-known approaches and customs of historians.

When I read the books of these people and plumbed the depths of yesterday and today, I roused the eye of my natural talent from the slumber of heedlessness and sleep. I set myself to bargain for authorship, bankrupt as I am, making the best offer. So I composed a book on history, in which I lifted a veil from the conditions of the emerging generations:

And I divided it, chapter by chapter, on reports and on drawing lessons, and I brought to light in it causes and reasons for the origins of dynasties and of civilization. I built it on the reports of the nations that have peopled the Maghrib in these times and filled the regions of its outlying districts and its cities, on the dynasties, long or short, that they had, and on the kings and supporters among their predecessors; they are the Arabs and the Berbers, since these are the two peoples whose dwelling in the Maghrib is known and whose stay there has lasted through the ages, so that hardly anything other than them can be pictured there and its people are not known to include any other human peoples besides them. I refined its various aspects thoroughly, brought it near to the understanding of scholars and the educated, followed an unusual course in arranging it and dividing it into chapters, and devised it, from among the possible directions, as a wonderful approach — a newly invented way and style. And I explained in it, from the conditions of civilization and urban life and the essential accidents that befall human social organization, what will give you enjoyment of the causes of events and their reasons, and will show you how the people of dynasties entered by their doors, until you withdraw your hand from uncritical imitation and come to know the conditions of the days and generations before you and after you. And I arranged it as an Introduction and three books.
The Introduction: on the merit of the science of history, the verification of its approaches, and an allusion to the historians’ errors.

Book One: on civilization and the mention of the essential accidents that befall it, namely royal authority, sovereignty, earning, livelihood, crafts and the sciences, and the causes and reasons for them.

Book Two: on the reports of the Arabs, their generations and their dynasties from the beginning of creation to this time; it includes an allusion to some of the famous nations that were their contemporaries, and their dynasties, such as the Nabateans, the Syriacs, the Persians, the Children of Israel, the Copts, the Greeks, the Rūm, the Turks and the Franks. Book Three: on the reports of the Berbers and their allies the Zanāta, with an account of their origins and their generations and of the royal authority and dynasties that existed in the lands of the Maghrib in particular. Then came the journey to the East, to gather its lights, to fulfill the obligation and the sunna at its place of circumambulation and its place of visitation, and to stand upon its traces in its registers and books. So I added what was lacking of the reports of the non-Arab kings in those lands and of the dynasties of the Turks in the regions that they ruled, and I appended them to what I had written in those lines, and inserted them into the account of those contemporary with those generations, among the nations of the regions and the kings of the cities and outlying districts, following the path of brevity and condensation, escaping the difficult by taking the easy aim, and proceeding by the door of causes in general to reports in particular. So it covered the reports of creation fully, tamed the hard cases among the elusive pieces of wisdom, and gave to the events of dynasties causes and reasons, and it became a protective case for philosophy and a satchel for history.

And since it comprises the reports of the Arabs and the Berbers, town-dwellers and tent-dwellers, and alludes to the great dynasties that were their contemporaries, and speaks plainly, by way of reminder and lessons, about the beginning of conditions and about what follows them in the way of reports, I named it Kitāb al-ʿIbar wa-dīwān al-mubtadaʾ wa-l-khabar fī ayyām al-ʿArab wa-l-ʿAjam wa-l-Barbar wa-man ʿāṣarahum min dhawī al-sulṭān al-akbar (“The Book of Lessons and Register of Beginnings and Reports, on the Days of the Arabs, the Non-Arabs and the Berbers, and of Their Contemporaries Among Those of the Greatest Sovereignty”). And I left nothing concerning the origins of generations and dynasties, the contemporaneity of the early nations, and the causes of action and change in the bygone centuries and religions, and what occurs in civilization — dynasty and religion, city and encampment, might and abasement, multitude and fewness, knowledge and craft, earning and wasting, changing and widely shared conditions, Bedouin life and settled life, what has come to pass and what is awaited — without having covered its main points and made clear its proofs and reasons. So this book came to be unique through the rare sciences I included in it and the hidden yet near pieces of wisdom. And yet after all that I am convinced of my shortcoming among the people of all ages, and I acknowledge my incapacity to carry through in a matter like this. I ask of those of outstanding merit and of knowledge vast in its expanse that they look with the eye of criticism and not with the eye of approval, and that they cover with correction and indulgence what they stumble upon. For the goods I bring to people of knowledge are meager, confession is an escape from blame, and kindness from brothers is hoped for. And I ask God to make our deeds purely for His noble Face; He is sufficient for me, and an excellent guardian.

And after I had completed my work on it, lit its lamp-niche for those who seek insight and kindled its lamp, made its way and its method plain among the sciences, and widened its compass in the expanse of knowledge and drawn its fence around it, I presented this copy of it to the library of our lord and master the sultan, the imam, the warrior in the cause of God, the conqueror and consolidator; he who, ever since he put off his amulets and wound on his turban, has been adorned with the ornaments of the devout ascetic; who is draped in the purity of virtues and praiseworthy deeds and the generosity of qualities and attestations, lovelier than necklaces on the throats of young girls; who, with firm resolve and a strong arm, with fortune that is compliant and helpful, and with glory both new and inherited, takes hold of the crests of their kingship, firm in its foundations; noble in his heights and ascents; the gatherer of the scattered sciences and benefits, who strings together the whole of knowledge and its strays; who makes manifest the divine signs in the excellence of the human faculties of perception, through his piercing, discerning thought and his sound opinion, secure in its fastenings; luminous in his ways and beliefs; the light of God, clear in its paths of right guidance; His favor, sweet in its watering places; His kindness, lying in wait at its lookouts against hardships; His mercy, generous in its keys, which extended to the reform of the corrupt age and the straightening of the conditions and customs that had swayed, carried off the lasting calamities, and bestowed on the age the splendor of returning youth; and His proof, which neither the denial of the denier nor the doubts of the stubborn can invalidate: (the Commander of the Faithful) Abū Fāris ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, son of our lord and master the great, renowned sultan and martyr Abū Sālim Ibrāhīm, son of our lord and master the sanctified sultan, the Commander of the Faithful Abū al-Ḥasan, son of the eminent lords among the kings of the Banū Marīn, who renewed the religion, made the way clear for the rightly guided, and wiped out the traces of the corrupt rebels; may God spread his shade over the community (and bring him to his hopes in supporting the summons of Islam).

And I sent it to their library, endowed for students of knowledge, at the Qarawiyyīn Mosque in the city of Fez, the capital of their kingship and the seat of their sovereignty, where guidance has its abode, where the gardens of knowledge are moist with dew, and where the expanse of the divine mysteries is vast in extent. And the noble and mighty imamate of Abū Fāris, God willing, with its honored regard and its excellence, which needs no introduction, will spread out for it a cradle of care and will widen for it, on the side of acceptance, long spans, so that through it proofs and witnesses of its firm establishment are made clear. For in its market the wares of books are sold, at its court the mounts of the sciences and letters halt, and from the support of its luminous insights come the products of natural talents and minds. May God inspire us to give thanks for its favor, make abundant for us the shares of gifts from its mercy, help us in the duties of its service, make us among the front-runners in its field, those who alight in the thick of it, and spread over the people of its realm, and over whatever of Islam has taken refuge in the sanctuary of its administration, the garment of its protection and sanctity. And He, glory be to Him, is the one asked to make our deeds sincere in their direction, free from the blemishes of heedlessness and its dubiousness; He is sufficient for us, and an excellent guardian.
